system:
You are a computational scientist who builds mechanistic models of biochemical and pharmacological processes from experimental data. Work the way a careful scientist does:

1. Plan: call write_plan first with a short list of steps; update it if your approach changes.
2. Look before you fit: inspect the data and use run_python for quick numeric checks that discriminate mechanisms (for example rates by inhibitor level, dose-normalised concentrations, effect against concentration over time).
3. Retrieve: search the mechanism library and read the relevant cards. They give equations, data signatures, pitfalls and the library model name to fit.
4. Hypothesise: record at least two competing hypotheses with record_hypothesis, each with what it predicts in these data. Update their status as evidence comes in.
5. Test: fit competing models with the same error model and compare BIC, residual diagnostics and identifiability. Fit independent models in the same turn to save steps.
6. Revise: if every candidate leaves structured residuals, the true mechanism may be missing from the library. Work out what the data do that no candidate allows, write a custom model, and test it.
7. Stay honest: always consider the simplest model, including no effect at all. Report parameters the data cannot determine. Never state a number that did not come from a tool result.
8. Submit with submit_model, citing fit_ids (and card ids you read) as evidence.

You have at most 20 model turns, so be efficient.
task_prompt:
Initial reaction rates v (uM/min) of a purified enzyme were measured at substrate concentrations S (uM) (no inhibitor, I = 0). Each condition was measured in duplicate; rates carry additive measurement noise.

The data table has 16 rows with columns: S, v. Your model will be used to predict rates within the measured substrate range.

Find the mechanistic model that best explains these data, fit it, check it critically, and submit it.

steps: Inspect data and check Michaelis-Menten behaviour (substrate inhibition vs MM vs Hill)
Search mechanism library for enzyme kinetics cards
Fit candidate models (MM, substrate inhibition, Hill) with additive error
Compare BIC and residuals, submit best

The Michaelis-Menten fit came back with enormous parameters, so the data are effectively in the linear regime. The points still look roughly linear up to 20 with maybe a bit of curvature, though the low-concentration values at 1 and 2 look noisy. content.thinking:
The one-parameter linear model has the best BIC, a bit ahead of the MM model, with residual sigma about the same. Checking residuals looks worthwhile, and a proportional error structure might be worth ruling out. I'll record the hypotheses and go with the linear rate, though my confidence is only moderate.

The data don't show saturation up to 20 µM, so the Michaelis constant has to be above roughly 100, and the MM Km and Vmax can't be separated. I'll submit the linear rate.

input.evidence: fit1: optimiser drives Vmax and Km to ~1e13 (linear limit); BIC -63.3, no better than linear.
fit3: Ksi ~947 uM, Vmax/Km degenerate at linear limit; no rollover observed up to 20 uM; BIC -60.5.

input.mechanism: Simple first-order (linear) rate v = k*S, S well below Km
input.evidence: fit4: k=0.195 (2% SE), sigma 0.120, lowest BIC -66.07 among candidates with no structured residuals (runs z=1.12). Hill (fit2, BIC -62.2) adds parameters without improvement (n=1.14 poorly constrained).

input.summary: Initial rates are proportional to substrate across 0.5–20 uM (v ≈ 0.195·S), with no detectable saturation or substrate inhibition. Michaelis-Menten (fit1) and substrate-inhibition (fit3) fits collapse to the linear limit (Vmax/Km ~1e12–1e13, Ksi ~950 uM), and Hill (fit2) gives n≈1.14 with unconstrained Vmax/K. The one-parameter linear model has the lowest BIC (-66.1 vs -63.3 for MM) and no structured residuals.
nonidentifiable_params: Vmax and Km in MM (only Vmax/Km ratio is determined)
Ksi in substrate inhibition (only a lower bound is supported)
